pages.text: Graphite is carbon in sheets, black, greasy and soft enough to write with.
pages.title: Graphite

pages.text: Flake graphite forms when the carbon in old mud and limestone is cooked in the deep crust, so it lies in schist and gneiss and marble: the flake mines of Heilongjiang, Mozambique's Balama and Madagascar work schist, and Sri Lanka's vein graphite fills cracks in gneiss.
Here it is a band of deepslate deep in any country, the flakes scattered through it.

Flake ore runs ten per cent carbon or so, and graphite floats: it repels water, so a little kerosene, the collector every graphite mill uses, carries the flakes up in the froth. Two raw graphite, 250 mB of water and 50 mB of kerosene under a mixer give a graphite concentrate, half the time two.
pages.title: Flotation and purification

pages.text: A concentrate is about 95 per cent carbon, the rest silicate. Hydrofluoric acid eats the silicate: two concentrate and 250 mB of it, heated, give two graphite, the 99.95 per cent the Chinese plants make.
Or burn it out: four concentrate under 100 mB of argon between three graphite electrodes in a firebrick-lined vat, past 2,500 °C, give four.
Synthetic graphite is Acheson's, from 1896: coke baked past 2,500 °C in an electric furnace orders itself into graphite. Two coal coke in the same arc vat give two graphite.
pages.title: Acheson and electrodes

pages.text: Graphite electrodes are made of it: four graphite and 100 mB of creosote, the pitch binder, pressed hot, give The Factory's graphite electrode, as its coke block cut on a stonecutter still does. Graphite is also the anode of every lithium-ion cell and the carbon layer of a tantalum capacitor.

Sources: USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Graphite (natural); Kogel and others, Industrial Minerals and Rocks, 7th ed. (SME, 2006), "Graphite"; Jara and others, "Purification, application and current market trend of natural graphite: a review", International Journal of Mining Science and Technology 29 (2019).
